questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the block dictates in direct carving
questions.learningObjective: Identify how the block constrains the finished carved form
questions.stem: A design brief asks for a granite lectern carved from a single quarried block. What limits the designer before any tool touches the stone?

options.text: The outer shape and volume of the block already restrict where the carving can go
Only the hardness of the granite decides the final form, since every block yields identically
options.misconception: ignores the original block volume as a limit

options.text: Nothing limits the designer, because a carver can cut a block into any shape at will
options.misconception: believes a carver can reshape a block without limit

options.text: The colour of the granite is the main constraint, since it decides how far carving may go
options.misconception: treats stone colour as the governing constraint

questions.explanation: Carving is subtractive, so the block's existing volume bounds every possible cut and the designer must read its faces and defects as part of the form. Hardness changes labour, not the composition.
questions.hint: Think about what is removed, not what is added.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Carving in the round against carving in relief
questions.learningObjective: Explain why relief and carving in the round differ in working time
questions.stem: A review tabulates carving budgets for two proposals: a free-standing figure at 400 hours and a wall panel at 260 hours, both from the same granite. Which explanation best accounts for the difference?

options.text: Relief carving needs less labour because the block for a panel is always a rarer, lower quality stone
options.misconception: assumes cheaper stone is the reason relief takes fewer hours

options.text: In relief the figure keeps a continuous backing, so the carver supports the shallow projection from the wall
Wall panels are carved entirely by apprentices, and skilled masons rarely work on relief work
options.misconception: assumes relief work is reserved for unskilled apprentices

options.text: The hours differ because free-standing figures must be hollowed out to keep their weight down
options.misconception: assumes free-standing carving requires hollowing for weight

questions.explanation: A relief keeps the original block behind the figure, so projections stay supported and undercutting is limited. Free-standing figures stand unsupported and need more finishing work.
questions.hint: Ask what holds the projection up from behind.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Subtractive against additive sculpture
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish subtractive making from additive making in a work
questions.stem: A conservation report compares an ashlar doorway cut from a single limestone block with a cast bronze insert assembled from wax and clay. Explain why the two objects belong to different categories of making.

answer.exemplar: The doorway is subtractive: the mason removes material from a solid block, so the finished form is bounded by the original stone and its grain. The bronze insert is additive and replicated: the sculptor builds up a wax model and this is translated into clay, plaster or metal, so the work can be enlarged and cast again.

questions.explanation: Subtractive work can only remove material, so block size and grain govern the result. Additive modelling builds up a form that can then be cast, which is what makes enlargement possible.
questions.hint: One process removes; the other adds and then copies.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the lost-wax process buys
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total workshop time a lost-wax casting requires
questions.stem: A foundry budgets 4 hours per kilogram for the wax model, 3 hours per kilogram for the mould, and 2 hours per kilogram for pouring and finishing. For a 25 kilogram bronze figure, how many hours in total?
questions.explanation: Each kilogram needs 4 plus 3 plus 2 equals 9 hours, and 9 times 25 kilograms gives 225 hours. A common error is to add the three rates without multiplying by weight, which yields only 9 hours.
questions.hint: Add the rates first, then multiply by the mass.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a mould does to the object it copies
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a cast reproduces surface detail in reverse

stimulus.body: The conservation team reports that a bronze group cast in the 1970s carries raised lines around every figure, including raised lettering on the plinth, running backwards. The original plaster model shows smooth surfaces and correctly oriented lettering.

questions.stem: Given the conservation report, what best explains the raised, reversed lettering on the cast?

options.text: The plinth was finished by hand after casting, and the finisher deliberately raised the lettering
options.misconception: assumes a finisher raised the lettering by hand

options.text: The mould was left in the furnace too long, and trapped gases raised every line during cooling
options.misconception: blames trapped gas for detail that comes from the mould

options.text: The mould inverted the model surface, so a cast reproduces detail in reverse and often raised
The original model itself was rough, and a later polish has hidden the smooth surfaces seen
options.misconception: blames the model rather than the casting process

questions.explanation: A casting copies the mould surface, and a mould taken from a model records its detail inversely, giving reversed and raised features. Bubbles or rough polishing would look irregular.
questions.hint: Ask what the mould recorded from the model surface.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the firing of clay limits
questions.learningObjective: Judge what a firing temperature permits in a casting workflow
questions.stem: A workshop wants a hollow clay form fired and then used as a mould for bronze. Stage one: the clay must be dried and fired to become permanent. Stage two: the fired form must then withstand molten bronze at about 1150 degrees. Given a kiln rated to 1000 degrees, what is the sound conclusion?

options.text: The rating matters only for decoration, since fired clay keeps its strength with molten metal indefinitely
options.misconception: dismisses the heat resistance of fired clay

options.text: The clay body must be fired well above 1000 degrees, which proves the stated kiln rating is wrong
options.misconception: treats the kiln rating as universally wrong

options.text: The fired clay will melt and run when it meets the bronze, so the casting step must be redesigned
options.misconception: claims fired clay melts on contact with bronze

options.text: The clay can be fired and used, but it will not survive contact with molten bronze without a refractory shell

questions.explanation: Firing makes clay permanent and heat resistant, but fired clay is unreliable against molten bronze near 1150 degrees. A 1000 degree kiln can fire the form, but casting needs a refractory shell.
questions.hint: Separate what the clay survives from what the bronze needs.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How the grain of a stone constrains carving
questions.learningObjective: Predict a structural failure caused by cutting across the grain
questions.stem: A brief warns that the block for a doorway lintel was cut across the grain. Which feature of the finished carving is most at risk from that choice?

options.text: A dull finish, because cross-cut stone cannot be polished to the sheen a lintel requires
options.misconception: confuses grain direction with polish quality

options.text: Long splits and weakness along the grain, which can open up as the lintel is carved and loaded
A change of colour, since cross-cutting exposes the interior of the stone and alters its tone
options.misconception: believes grain direction alters the colour of stone

options.text: An inability to carve any detail, since cross-cut stone refuses to take a chisel at all
options.misconception: believes cross-cut stone cannot be carved at all

questions.explanation: Stone is weakest along the grain, so a lintel cut across it risks splitting under the chisel and later under load. Grain direction does not change colour or stop a carver working it.
questions.hint: Think about where the stone naturally splits.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the block dictates in direct carving
questions.learningObjective: Select the block that a direct carving brief can safely use
questions.stem: A quarry spreadsheet compares two blocks: Block A measures 1.2 by 0.8 by 0.6 metres with sound grain, Block B measures 1.6 by 0.9 by 0.5 metres with a hidden fracture. Which block suits a direct carving brief and why?

options.text: Neither, because a carver requires a block with no parallel faces to cut a figure in the round
options.misconception: invents a rule that blocks need no parallel faces

options.text: Block B, because its larger footprint lets the carver orient the figure to hide the fracture
options.misconception: assumes a larger block can simply hide a fracture

options.text: Block A, because its unbroken volume and sound grain give the carver material without a hidden failure plane
Both equally, because a hidden fracture only matters after the carving is finished and installed
options.misconception: ignores fractures as a factor in the carving process

questions.explanation: Direct carving needs sound stone, since every cut exposes the interior and a fracture can split the piece later. Block A offers workable volume without a hidden failure plane.
questions.hint: Ask which block is safe to cut into.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Carving in the round against carving in relief
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a relief and a figure in the round relate to their ground
questions.stem: A museum educator asks why a relief panel and a figure carved in the round look different in the weight of their shadows. Explain the difference in how each form relates to its ground.

answer.exemplar: A relief is carved in shallow projection from a continuous background, so the figure is still attached to the block and casts a low shadow onto that same surface. A figure carved in the round stands free of any background, so it is modelled on all sides and casts a shadow that moves fully around it.

questions.explanation: In relief the figure and its ground stay one piece, so the shadow lies flat against the block. In the round the figure is detached, so the shadow travels around it and the back must be modelled too.
questions.hint: Ask whether the figure and its background are one piece.

questions.topic: Subtractive against additive sculpture
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the volume of material removed by a subtractive carving
questions.stem: A brief specifies a marble block of 0.80 by 0.60 by 0.50 metres for a carved figure. After carving, the finished figure measures 0.40 by 0.30 by 0.25 metres. How many cubic metres of marble were removed?
questions.explanation: The block holds 0.8 times 0.6 times 0.5 equals 0.24 cubic metres; the figure holds 0.4 times 0.3 times 0.25 equals 0.03. The difference of 0.21 is the marble removed.
questions.hint: Volume removed is block volume minus figure volume.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the lost-wax process buys
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the lost-wax process makes possible that carving cannot

stimulus.body: The foundry log records that a bronze figure modelled in clay was sent to a moulding shop, where a wax version was taken from the clay. The wax was covered in investment, burned out, and the cavity filled with molten bronze. A small wax sprue was cast into the base and later cut away.

questions.stem: Given the foundry note, what does the lost-wax process make possible that direct carving cannot?

options.text: A single bronze object whose shape was never preceded by any model of clay or wax
options.misconception: thinks the casting can exist without any prior model

options.text: A surface that carries every fingerprint and thumbprint left by the original clay modeller
options.misconception: believes the casting preserves the modeller's fingerprints

options.text: A casting that is lighter than the clay original, since bronze expands during the pour
options.misconception: claims bronze expands during pouring and lightens the cast

options.text: An edition of near-identical bronze casts, each made from a fresh mould taken from the same model

questions.explanation: Because wax is replaced by metal in a repeatable process, each casting repeats the same model, so editions are possible. Bronze does not expand when poured, and the surface comes from the mould.
questions.hint: Ask what the destroyed wax model allows later.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a mould does to the object it copies
questions.learningObjective: Explain why repeated use of a mould alters later castings
questions.stem: Stage one: a foundry reuses one plaster mould for 40 small bronze castings. Stage two: the quality manager notices that the 40th casting shows a slightly softened and flattened version of the model's fine features. What best explains the outcome?

options.text: The bronze became too cold at the 40th pour, so the metal froze before it filled the finest cavities
options.misconception: blames cold metal for mould surface wear

options.text: Each casting wore down the mould surface, so repeated use slowly smoothed and widened the recorded detail
The wax model was worn by handling in the studio, so the model itself supplied a poorer mould each week
options.misconception: blames the studio model rather than the mould for the change

options.text: The investment plaster was mixed for too long, so its setting time grew and the mould lagged the model
options.misconception: invents an investment setting problem as the cause

questions.explanation: Molten metal abrades the cavity at each pour, so repeated castings reproduce an increasingly softened surface. Progressive loss of fine relief points to mould wear, not a cold pour.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a cavity after many pours.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the firing of clay limits
questions.learningObjective: Explain how firing fixes the colour range available to a ceramic body
questions.stem: A brief specifies a ceramic balustrade for a garden terrace. What does the firing limit for clay mean for the balustrade's colour range?

options.text: Colour varies only with the thickness of the applied glaze and not with the body or the atmosphere
options.misconception: denies that firing atmosphere affects the final colour

options.text: Any colour is possible after firing, because heat can turn a pale clay into any chosen hue
options.misconception: believes firing alone can produce any chosen colour

options.text: The body colour is fixed by the clay and firing atmosphere, so the range lies in the glazes
The firing fixes the colour permanently so that no later glaze or treatment can change it
options.misconception: believes firing blocks all later surface treatments

questions.explanation: Body colour is set by the clay minerals and by whether the kiln atmosphere is oxidising or reducing. Firing cannot make an arbitrary hue, but glazes can cover a wide colour range.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the piece the glazes control.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How the grain of a stone constrains carving
questions.learningObjective: Specify a cutting direction from measured strength data
questions.stem: A test report records tensile strengths for two limestone samples from one quarry: Sample P, taken parallel to the bedding, fails at 8 megapascals; Sample Q, taken across it, fails at 3 megapascals. What should the brief specify?

options.text: That the weaker sample be used for panels, since a softer stone resists weathering better
options.misconception: confuses softness with resistance to weathering

options.text: That all elements be cut across the bedding, because cross-cut stone takes a finer chisel finish
options.misconception: recommends cross-cutting for finish rather than strength

options.text: That the choice of cutting direction is irrelevant, since strength values apply equally in every direction
options.misconception: ignores the measured difference between the two samples

options.text: That load-bearing elements be cut parallel to the bedding, where the stone resists splitting best

questions.explanation: The parallel sample carries far more load before failing, matching the way stone splits along its bedding. Cutting direction therefore decides how the element behaves in service.
questions.hint: Compare the two failure loads directly.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the block dictates in direct carving
questions.learningObjective: Explain the meaning carried by an untouched quarry face
questions.stem: A client asks why the sculptor chooses to leave one face of the granite plinth exactly as the quarry split it. Explain what this choice contributes to the reading of a direct carving.

answer.exemplar: A direct carving is read as the block's own form being revealed rather than imposed from outside. Leaving one split face untouched keeps the raw material visibly present and states that the mass, weight and structure of the original block remain the source of the work, while the carved faces show the deliberate decisions made inside it.

questions.explanation: An untouched quarry face keeps the block's origin and weight legible, so the work reads as shaped within a mass rather than assembled. Split and worked surfaces then carry that meaning.
questions.hint: Ask what the untouched face says about the material.

questions.topic: Carving in the round against carving in relief
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the extra cost of carving in the round against relief
questions.stem: A brief allows a carver 60 hours to finish a wall relief and 90 hours to finish the same figure carved in the round. How many more hours does the free-standing version need, as a percentage of the relief budget?
questions.explanation: The difference is 90 minus 60 equals 30 hours, and 30 over 60 gives one half, so the free-standing version costs 50 percent more. Comparing against the round budget would wrongly give 33 percent.
questions.hint: Divide the extra hours by the relief budget.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Subtractive against additive sculpture
questions.learningObjective: Compare what can still be altered on site in each process

stimulus.body: Two proposals arrive for a civic plinth. The first proposes a bronze group cast from a wax model. The second proposes a limestone mass cut down from a single block by a carver in the yard. The committee notes that only the second proposal can be altered on site once work has begun.

questions.stem: Given the committee's note about on-site alteration, which statement about the two proposals is correct?

options.text: The cast bronze can be adjusted on site by welding, whereas the carved limestone cannot be changed
options.misconception: claims bronze is endlessly repairable and stone is not

options.text: The carved limestone can be adjusted on site by cutting, while the cast bronze is corrected in the foundry
Both proposals can be changed on site, since casting and carving both leave the surface open
options.misconception: assumes casting leaves the surface as open as carving

options.text: Neither proposal can be changed on site, because carving and casting are both completed before departure
options.misconception: claims both processes finish before leaving the workshop

questions.explanation: Carving leaves the block on site with uncut material still available, so adjustments can be made with tools. A cast bronze is finished once it leaves the foundry, so corrections happen there.
questions.hint: Ask which process still has raw material available.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the lost-wax process buys
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the lost-wax sequence preserves about the model
questions.stem: Stage one: a designer wants a bronze version of a small clay maquette. Stage two: the pattern maker sets out three castings, one original and two later copies. What does the process make straightforward in this case?

options.text: Reusing the original clay maquette afterwards, since the wax stage never takes material from it
options.misconception: believes the wax stage never touches the original model

options.text: Producing a bronze with a totally different surface texture, since the metal records the mould differently
options.misconception: invents a change of surface texture between clay and bronze

options.text: Reproducing the maquette at the same size, since the wax and mould stages transfer the model's dimensions
Cutting the clay maquette in half to see its interior, since the mould stage is fully transparent
options.misconception: suggests the mould stage allows the model to be cut open

questions.explanation: The wax stage records the maquette accurately, so the mould reproduces the model's dimensions at the same scale. The original clay is not consumed, and the metal carries the mould's surface.
questions.hint: Ask whether scale changes between the stages.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a mould does to the object it copies
questions.learningObjective: Define the mould as a negative copy that fixes surface character
questions.stem: A conservator explains why the surface of a cast bronze is smoother than the clay model beneath it. What is the real relationship between the mould and the object it produces?

options.text: The mould is a soft lining that is entirely replaced by the bronze during the pouring process
options.misconception: claims the mould material is fully replaced by the metal

options.text: The mould is a positive copy that adds its own texture to the metal as the bronze cools
options.misconception: treats the mould as a positive that adds its own texture

options.text: The mould is only a container for the metal and has no effect on the finished surface
options.misconception: believes the mould container has no effect on the surface

options.text: The mould is a negative copy that fixes surface detail and gives every casting from it the same character

questions.explanation: The mould is a negative that inverts the model's surface into a cavity, and that recorded surface transfers to the metal. It does not add texture; it fixes the texture every casting carries.
questions.hint: Ask whether the mould adds or reproduces surface.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the firing of clay limits
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a kiln log that records different firing temperatures
questions.stem: A kiln log records three firings: a low-fire earthenware firing topping 900 degrees, a stoneware firing at 1250 degrees, and a third at 1000 degrees that produced soft, porous bodies. What does the log indicate?

options.text: That the third firing must have run hotter than the second, because soft porous bodies indicate overheating
options.misconception: misreads soft porous bodies as evidence of overheating

options.text: That firing temperature sets how vitrified and durable the body becomes, and 1000 degrees sits below the range
That firing temperature has no bearing on body strength, since all three batches share the same clay
options.misconception: denies any link between temperature and body density

options.text: That colour alone determined the outcome, since the third batch was fired in a reducing atmosphere
options.misconception: explains the result by atmosphere instead of temperature

questions.explanation: As the firing peak rises, the body vitrifies and densifies, so hardness and durability increase. The soft porous result shows the third firing stopped short of the vitrifying range.
questions.hint: Ask what the third batch's softness tells you.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How the grain of a stone constrains carving
questions.learningObjective: Explain why tooling direction follows the bedding of stone
questions.stem: An engineer argues that a limestone cornice must be tooled in the direction of the bedding rather than across it. Explain the reason for that instruction in terms of how the stone fails.

answer.exemplar: Stone fails most readily along its bedding planes, where the mineral layers are weakest and most nearly separated. Tooling in that direction leaves a surface lying across the beds and encourages the carver's strokes to run with the grain, reducing the risk of a clean split along the course. Working against the bedding would drive the tool into the weak layers and open hidden planes beneath the finish.

questions.explanation: Because stone splits most easily along its bedding, working in that direction keeps the surface crossing the weak layers rather than following them. Working against the bedding opens hidden splits.
questions.hint: Ask along which plane the stone wants to part.

questions.topic: Carving in the round against carving in relief
questions.learningObjective: Deduce how a relief with a continuous background was produced

stimulus.body: An eighteenth-century marble relief shows a battle scene with figures overlapping in shallow layers. A laboratory comparison notes that no part of the relief is free of the background slab, and the deepest projection measures about a quarter of the figure's width.

questions.stem: Given the collection note about the unbroken background, which conclusion follows about the way the relief was made?

options.text: The figures were painted onto a flat surface, since the projections carry no carved tool marks
options.misconception: claims the projection is painted rather than carved

options.text: The figures were modelled separately and then fixed to the slab, since the depth matches a free-standing model
options.misconception: mistakes the shallow projection for separate modelling

options.text: The figures were cut back from a continuous slab, so the remaining background defines their edges
The figures were cast from a mould in one pour, since the unbroken slab points to a single casting
options.misconception: attributes the slab to casting rather than carving

questions.explanation: A continuous background behind every figure means the work was cut down from one slab, with shapes emerging from the material left standing. Casting would not bond figures to one field.
questions.hint: Ask how the edges of the figures are made.

questions.topic: Subtractive against additive sculpture
questions.learningObjective: Identify the stage that makes enlargement possible
questions.stem: Stage one: a brief asks the sculptor to produce a clay model that a foundry can enlarge three times. Stage two: the foundry casts the three bronzes. Which step actually sets the possibility of enlargement?

options.text: The firing stage, because clay becomes permanently rigid only after firing and can then be scaled
options.misconception: claims rigidity after firing is what makes scaling possible

options.text: The subtractive carving stage, because a stone block can be measured and cut to a larger scale
options.misconception: credits subtraction with the capacity to enlarge a work

options.text: The final polishing stage, because polish makes a model measurable and therefore reproducible
options.misconception: mistakes polishing for the step that enables measurement

options.text: The additive modelling stage, because a model built up in clay can be measured and reproduced at larger scale

questions.explanation: Enlargement needs a model apart from the finished object, so a form built up in clay can be measured and reproduced. Subtractive carving is tied to its block, and firing changes nothing about that.
questions.hint: Ask which process produces a separate model.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the specific advantage of modelling in wax before casting
questions.stem: A teaching note asks what the lost-wax process buys the sculptor compared with carving directly in stone. Which benefit is specific to that process?

options.text: A finished surface that needs no chasing, patination or polishing after the metal has been cast
options.misconception: believes casting removes the need for surface finishing

options.text: The chance to revise the form in a soft medium before committing to an expensive and irreversible material
A guarantee that every casting from the same mould will be dimensionally identical to the last
options.misconception: claims identical moulds guarantee identical castings

options.text: The ability to add material to the bronze after casting, so corrections can be poured in afterwards
options.misconception: thinks corrections can simply be cast into the metal later

questions.explanation: Working in wax or clay lets the sculptor alter the form while it is cheap and reversible, which is unavailable once stone is cut. Castings still need finishing, and pours vary slightly.

questions.topic: What a mould does to the object it copies
questions.learningObjective: Compare the fidelity of a rigid and a flexible mould
questions.stem: A foundry compares two moulds taken from the same clay model. Mould A is plaster, cast in a closed two-part form. Mould B is a flexible latex skin made from the same model. Which difference in surface result follows from this?

options.text: Both moulds will record the model identically, because the parting line affects the metal and not the mould
options.misconception: believes the parting line has no effect on the mould surface

options.text: Mould A should carry the model texture better, because rigid plaster holds a parting line cleanly
options.misconception: assumes rigid plaster records finer detail than soft skin

options.text: Mould B should carry the model texture better, because a flexible skin follows contours with no parting line
Neither mould records texture at all, because texture is a property of the original model alone
options.misconception: claims texture belongs to the model and is never recorded

questions.explanation: A flexible skin moulds closely around the model and avoids a parting line cutting across the surface, so it holds fine texture better. Rigid plaster needs a seam and can soften small modelled marks.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the firing of clay limits
questions.learningObjective: Explain how firing constrains the wall thickness a potter chooses
questions.stem: A client wants a large ceramic vase that must later be lifted by four people without flexing. Explain what the firing process imposes on the wall thickness the potter should choose.

answer.exemplar: Firing drives off bound water and sinters the clay particles into a rigid, vitrified body, and this irreversible set happens while the piece is still inside the kiln. A wall that is too thin, or that dries unevenly, will warp or crack as it shrinks and vitrifies, and no amount of careful handling later will straighten it. The potter must therefore choose a thickness that survives shrinking and vitrification before the piece is ever handled.

questions.explanation: Firing is irreversible: clay shrinks and sinters as it heats, and any warping is locked in at that point. Wall thickness must survive that shrinkage, because nothing can be corrected afterwards.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a warp after the kiln.

questions.topic: What the block dictates in direct carving
questions.learningObjective: Judge a block with a natural cleft against a load path

stimulus.body: The stone for the gateway pier was specified as a single block with no jointing allowed. Site notes record that the quarry delivered a block with a natural cleft running diagonally across the upper half. The mason asks whether to accept it or to split it into two pieces.

questions.stem: Given the site note about the diagonal cleft, what should the mason do?

options.text: Turn the block so the cleft runs vertical, because a vertical cleft cannot carry any lateral force
options.misconception: assumes orientation removes the lateral force on a cleft

options.text: Accept the block, because a diagonal cleft is hidden by the finished facing and adds useful character
options.misconception: treats a hidden cleft as a benefit rather than a weakness

options.text: Accept the block and fill the cleft with mortar, since mortar will bond the two halves into one mass
options.misconception: believes mortar can bond a natural cleft into solid mass

options.text: Reject or split the block, because a natural cleft crossing the load path can open under the weight above

questions.explanation: A natural cleft is a pre-existing plane of weakness, and if it crosses the load path the weight above can split the block. Mortar hides the problem without removing the plane of failure.
questions.hint: Ask what the cleft does once the load arrives.

questions.topic: Subtractive against additive sculpture

Additive practice belongs to soft materials only, while subtractive practice belongs to hard materials
options.misconception: ties the terms to material hardness rather than to process

questions.explanation: The distinction is about direction of working: material added or taken away. Casting transfers a finished form into another material, so it can carry either a modelled or a carved form.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a mould does to the object it copies
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two castings from one model differ in fidelity
questions.stem: A design team asks why two castings from the same mould can be sold at different prices. Explain what makes one casting a more exact record of the model than the other.

answer.exemplar: A casting is only as faithful as the cavity that held the metal, and that cavity is itself a copy of the model made in a material that wears. If the mould was taken carefully and used only a few times, the mould surface still carries the model's finest lines, and the metal picks them up. If the mould has been reused until its detail is rounded off, the bronze inherits that rounding, so the two castings differ in the accuracy of the record rather than in their identity.

questions.explanation: Fidelity passes through the mould, which wears and softens with each pour. The casting made early from a fresh mould records the model more exactly than one made after the cavity lost detail.
questions.hint: Ask how many times the mould was used.

options.misconception: believes grouting can change the bedding of stone

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the lost-wax process buys
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the wax pattern is destroyed during casting
questions.stem: A foundry foreman explains why the original wax model is destroyed during casting. Explain what the destruction allows the casting process to achieve.

answer.exemplar: The wax has to melt out of the investment shell to leave a hollow cavity that the bronze can occupy, and that is exactly why a wax version is used rather than a solid metal pattern. Melting the wax also frees the sculptor from any awkwardness of a rigid pattern being lifted out of a mould, since the material simply drains away. The metal takes the space the wax held, so the model survives in bronze as a surface and a form while the wax itself is gone.

questions.explanation: Wax melts out of the investment to leave a cavity for the metal, which is why wax is the practical pattern material. The bronze occupies exactly the space the wax held, so the model survives as form.
questions.hint: Ask what space the metal must fill.

options.misconception: assumes two separate glazes were applied and fired

options.text: Flame contact oxidised the exposed side, the atmosphere altered the sheltered one, and salts vaporised there
The vessel was turned in the kiln mid firing, so the flame marked the surface facing the door

options.text: The brown came from iron in the clay burning, while the bloom is water trapped between wall and glaze
options.misconception: explains the bloom as trapped water rather than salts

options.misconception: reduces grain direction to a matter of appearance only

options.text: The cheaper block is acceptable, because granite is strong enough that grain direction makes no difference

Either block works, because the mortar bedding joint is stronger than the stone in both directions

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Subtractive against additive sculpture
questions.learningObjective: Compare two routes that produce the same outline
questions.stem: A design workshop asks the participants to compare building a wall from stacked blocks with modelling a wall surface in wet clay. Explain what distinguishes the two ways of producing the same outline.

answer.exemplar: The stacked-block wall and the modelled clay wall can share an outline, but they arrive at it by opposite routes. Stacking assembles a surface from separate units, each one placed and then locked to its neighbours by the weight and mortar above it. Modelling builds one continuous surface by adding and smoothing material, so the shape emerges from the inside of the mass rather than from a sequence of fitted parts. The first is assembled from parts, the second is continuous, and they fail in different ways.

questions.explanation: One produces a surface by fitting separate units together, the other by building a continuous mass that is then shaped. The outline may match, but the internal structure differs entirely.
questions.hint: Ask how each surface comes into being.

Because the marble surface was sanded before moulding, so only the deepest cuts were recorded and reversed

questions.explanation: A mould records the surface as an inverted cavity, so a cut in the marble becomes a projection in the metal. Pouring speed, polishing and sanding change finish but not that reversal.

questions.topic: Carving in the round against carving in relief

questions.stem: A conservator asks why the shadow cast by a relief changes with the direction of the light while the shadow of a free-standing figure changes its length and position. Explain the difference in terms of what each form touches.

answer.exemplar: The shadow of a relief stays on the surface that carries it, because the figure and its background are one continuous mass and the shadow can only fall a short distance behind the projecting form. A figure carved in the round is detached from any background, so light from one side throws its shadow onto the floor, a wall or empty space at a distance, and that shadow travels around the object as the light source moves. The difference is therefore a difference in contact.

questions.explanation: A relief's shadow lands on the same slab that supports the figure, so it stays attached and close. A free-standing figure throws its shadow onto other things entirely.
questions.hint: Ask what surface receives the shadow.

questions.topic: What the lost-wax process buys

stimulus.body: A bronze replica is cast from a clay model, and the foundry will not return the original clay. The client's contract, however, lists the clay model among the items to be delivered with the finished work, and the model was modelled at full size.

questions.stem: Given the foundry's practice and the contract, how can the client's requirement be met?

options.text: By explaining to the client that the clay cannot be preserved, since bronze contracts as it cools
options.misconception: invents a metal contraction as the reason the clay was lost

options.text: By delivering a bronze cast of the model, since it is geometrically identical to the clay in every respect
options.misconception: claims a cast is in every measurable respect like the clay

options.misconception: treats the investment shell as an acceptable substitute

options.text: By delivering a second wax taken from the original clay before it was destroyed, preserving form and scale

questions.explanation: Because the clay is destroyed in the foundry, the only way to keep a full-size model is to take a wax from it before casting. A bronze cast is a copy of the model, and the investment is only a shell.
questions.hint: Ask what can be taken from the clay before casting.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a mould does to the object it copies
questions.learningObjective: Assess what casting makes easy and what it makes hard
questions.stem: Stage one: a museum commissions six identical bronze editions of a small figure. Stage two: after two years the museum wants to add a further three editions. What does the process make easy and what does it make hard?

options.text: Adding editions is hard because the mould is destroyed in casting, while reproducing the earlier casts is easy
options.misconception: claims the mould is destroyed and that duplication is easy

options.text: Adding editions is easy because the mould can be reused, but reproducing earlier casts exactly is hard
Both are easy, since every casting from the same model is by definition an exact duplicate
options.misconception: assumes every casting from one model is an exact duplicate

options.text: Both are hard, since the model itself is altered by the first casting it produces
options.misconception: claims the model is altered by being cast

questions.explanation: Casting supports multiplication, since a surviving mould can be used again. Exact repetition is harder, because each pour abrades the cavity and later editions carry a softened record of the model.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the cavity with each pour.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the firing of clay limits
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a second firing acts on an already fired body
questions.stem: A ceramic engineer explains why a clay body that has been fired once behaves differently in a second firing. What is the correct account of that change?

options.text: The first firing softens the body completely, so the second firing simply restores it to its original state
options.misconception: claims the first firing leaves the body fully soft again

options.text: The first firing removes all the chemically active clay, so the second firing has no material left to work on
options.misconception: claims the first firing removes the material entirely

options.text: The first firing sinters and partly vitrifies the body, so the second acts on an already rigid material
The first firing sets the final colour, so any further firing can only darken or burn the piece
options.misconception: claims the colour is fixed and cannot be affected further

questions.explanation: Firing sinters the body and fuses part of it, so a second firing acts on a material that is no longer raw clay. Colour can still shift and the body is not consumed.
questions.hint: Ask what the first firing did to the particles.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How the grain of a stone constrains carving
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the difference in failure counts between two cutting directions
questions.stem: A test series records how many samples failed under bending: 2 of 40 cut parallel to the bedding and 14 of 40 cut across it. How many more failures occurred in the cross-cut group?
questions.explanation: The cross-cut group recorded 14 failures and the parallel group recorded 2, so the difference is 12. The parallel group failed far less often, which supports cutting parallel to the bedding.
questions.hint: Subtract the parallel failures from the cross-cut ones.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the block dictates in direct carving
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the intended view must be settled before cutting
questions.stem: A designer asks why the intended view of a carving has to be decided before the block is cut. Explain what the decision controls.

answer.exemplar: The block is cut with a bed, a grain and a set of dimensions, and once the first cut is made those are fixed. Choosing the view in advance therefore decides where the mass of the stone will lie and how the figure will be read, because a carving made to be seen from the front carries its detail on that face and simplifies what it cannot show. Deciding later forces the carver to solve the problem with tools that cannot recover the lost mass of the block.

questions.explanation: The block's mass, bed and grain are fixed at the first cut, so the intended view determines how the form is distributed. Choosing later forces the carver to remove mass that cannot be recovered.
questions.hint: Ask what is fixed by the first cut.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Carving in the round against carving in relief
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the proportion of height taken by the deepest relief projection
questions.stem: A sculptor carves a relief 0.6 metres high with a maximum projection of 0.12 metres. As a fraction of the height, what is the maximum projection?
questions.explanation: Dividing the projection of 0.12 metres by the height of 0.6 metres gives 0.2, so the deepest projection is one fifth of the overall height. This shallowness keeps the figure bonded to its background.
questions.hint: Divide the projection by the overall height.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Subtractive against additive sculpture
questions.learningObjective: Identify what is lost when only the finished surface is documented

stimulus.body: During an installation, the stone carver for the memorial wall departs and is replaced by a fabricator who works from digital drawings and CNC machinery. The drawings specify the finished wall surface only, with no record of the working method that would have been used to cut it.

questions.stem: Given the site memo about the switch to CNC fabrication, what is lost when only the finished surface is specified?

options.text: The weight of the wall, since digitally cut panels are invariably lighter than hand-worked stone
options.misconception: invents a weight difference between machined and hand stone

options.text: The accuracy of the finished wall, since a machine cannot match a mason's line to the same tolerance
options.misconception: claims the machine cannot hold the same tolerance

options.text: The surface finish, since cut stone always carries more tool evidence than a machined one
options.misconception: claims the surface finish is necessarily inferior

options.text: The record of the subtractive working, since the finished surface alone does not show how the block was cut

questions.explanation: Specifying only the surface records the outcome without the method, and how the block was worked is part of what the object documents. Accuracy and finish depend on tolerances and tooling.
questions.hint: Ask whether the record shows the making or only the result.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the lost-wax process buys
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the factor by which a casting enlarges a maquette
questions.stem: A foundry plans a full size bronze figure from a clay maquette standing 30 centimetres tall. The finished bronze measures 1.5 metres. By what factor is the bronze larger than the maquette?
questions.explanation: Converting both to centimetres gives 150 and 30, and 150 divided by 30 equals 5, so the bronze is five times the height of the maquette. Mould and casting carry the model across that change of scale.
questions.hint: Put both heights in the same unit before dividing.
